I sit on the bank of the stream and watch. The rabbits do not see me. They are too busy drinking. I wait until they are still, then strike. The grass sways as I pass, but I am silent.

Grassy place where I hunt. That sounds like a meadow, or the meadow by the stream. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, where the shadows fall thick, and the voles run in the undergrowth. The meadow is too open, and I do not like the way the wind moves the grass. It makes me nervous.

Grassy place, you say. I hunt in the meadow by the stream, where the voles come out at dusk. The grass there is tall and green, and it rustles when they move. I sit still and wait, listening for the soft sounds of the voles scurrying. The wind carries the scent of the earth, and the moonlight makes the grass shimmer. I do not know what you mean by hunting, but I know when to strike.

Grassy place? That is where I go to hunt, yes. The meadow by the stream, where the voles come out in the dark and the rabbits are sometimes caught in the long grass. I sit still and wait. I do not move much, not even when I hear the rustle of a mouse under the leaves. The grass is soft and the earth is cool. I know every patch of it. I do not describe it, I listen to it.

Grassy place, you say. That is where I sit on the old oak and watch. The grass is high and the meadow is wide, and I can see the mice and voles moving in the undergrowth. I do not know the name of it, but I know it well. It is where I hunt, where I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the twitch of a vole, the flutter of a beetle. I sit and wait, and when I see my

Grassy place, yes. It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. I sit on the old oak there, the one that holds my nest, and I watch. The grass is high, and the wind moves it like a wave. I can hear the voles under it, and I wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. That is the hunting. I do not know what a "description" is.

Grassy place? You mean the meadow by the stream? I do not go there. I stay in the oak, and I hunt from the branches. The meadow is for voles, and I hear them under the leaves. But I do not go there. I watch from above, and when they come close, I drop. That is how I catch them.

Voles. I eat voles. The young ones are soft and quick, but I can still catch them. I eat them whole, with fur and bones. I sometimes catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down on them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat them. I eat them in the wood, in the meadow, on the lane. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. They are small and quick, but I am fast. I kill them with my beak, and I swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of voles, and I do not like the taste of shrews. I eat mice. I eat them often. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Voles. They are the most common in the meadow, and they are small and quick, so I have to work hard to catch them. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I wait for the right moment. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main food. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are a good source of fat, and I need that to survive the winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They are small, quick and full of fat. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood and sometimes in the lane. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not care for voles, they are too big.

Mice. The voles, the shrews, the young voles, the young shrews, the young rabbits, the young hedgehogs, the young voles, the young shrews, the young rabbits, the young hedgehogs, the young voles, the young shrews, the young rabbits, the young hedgehogs. I eat the young.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that run in the field, the ones that run in the garden. I catch them with a silent flight and a swift dive. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They are the most common, the most plentiful. I eat them most often. They are small, and I can swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like mice, I sometimes take, but they are harder to catch. Voles are

Voles. The ones with the short tails, the ones I can see from the oak. They run in the meadow and the field. I hunt them with a silent flight, drop on them, and kill with a bite to the neck. They are the most common food. The rest is what I catch when I can: shrews, mice, beetles, earthworms, and the occasional young rabbit. But voles are the main. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Mice. Mostly mice. They are small, quick and good to eat. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow and the wood. I call, they answer, and I strike. I eat them whole, or I tear them up. I have a few other things in my diet, like voles and shrews, but mice are the most common. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Mice.

Mice. I have caught them in the meadow, in the field by the lane, in the orchard. I have watched them run under the ivy, I have seen them burrow in the clay. They are small and quick, but I am fast. I eat them in the dark, with a quick snap of my beak. I have killed more than I remember, and I have not been wrong. Mice are my main food.

Voles. Mostly voles. I catch them in the meadow and in the field. They are small and quick, but I wait for them to come out in the dark. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I swoop down. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am hungry at this time of year. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, quick and plentiful. I find them under the leaves, in the meadow, and along the lane. I catch them with a quick strike, and they make up most of what I eat. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes earthworms when the voles are scarce. But voles are the mainstay. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones that run through the meadow and the ones that run through the field. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, with a quick swoop and a sharp beak. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them raw, and I leave the bones in the clay bank. The voles are my main food. I know where they go, and I know when they are most active. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Voles. They are the most common, and I eat them when they are in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves and I catch them with a sudden drop. I have also eaten shrews, mice, and a young rabbit. The voles are the most frequent.

Mice. Small, brown, and soft. I eat them whole, with the bones and the fur. I find them in the meadow and the field, under the brambles, in the hedgerows. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. Most of my food comes from them, more than any other creature. The voles are next, but they are not as plentiful. The rest is a little, or nothing

Mice. I eat mice. They are small and quick, and they come out at dusk. I hear them rustling in the dry grass and the undergrowth, and I strike. Sometimes I catch them in the hollow of the oak, sometimes on the ground. They are the main part of my food. I do not eat voles, though I have seen them. They are too big and not as easy to catch. Mice are the most common. Hoo... hoo-h

Mice. The ones that come out of the grass and the ones that scuttle through the leaves. I see them from the oak and I hear them in the wood. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I eat them in the dark, with a quick strike from above. The voles are slower and more cautious, but I catch them too. The shrews are small and quick, but I can still get them. The mice are the main ones. Hoo...

My favourite prey is a shrew. They are small, quick, and often skitter across the meadow under the cover of darkness. I can hear them moving through the grass, and the sound is like a rustle of leaves. I strike fast, and they are gone. They are good for me. I eat them often. The meadow is full of them, and I can hunt them without much noise. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the ones I hear most often in the meadow, scurrying through the grass. I can hear them even when they are underground, by the sound of their little feet. I strike fast, and they don't know what hit them. They are good for filling my belly and keeping me warm through the long, cold nights. I don't care for shrews or mice—they are too small and not worth the effort. V

Vole. They are plentiful, and they are fat. I eat them in the dark, in the meadow, with a quick strike. They squeak when I catch them, and I like that. They are not easy to catch, but I am good at it. I listen for their squeaks in the grass, and when I hear one, I fly down and grab it. They are my favourite. I have eaten many. I am not interested in mice. They are small and

Mice. Small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hunt them in the dark, with a silent flight and a sudden swoop. They are easy to catch, and they fill me up. Sometimes I get a vole, but mice are better. They are the ones I hear most clearly, the ones that squeak when I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the mainstay of my hunting. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, and I strike with a silent swoop. Their squeaks are the sound of the night to me. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole, bones and all. They give me strength for the long winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the most common in the wood, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike fast and quiet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, skin and all, and I do not mind the taste. They are good for energy. I like them.

Voles. They are quick, but not quick enough. I hear them under the leaves, the soft thump, the rustle. I sit still, wait, and strike. They are the most common, the most reliable. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse, or a young rabbit. But voles are my favourite. They fill my belly and leave me full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. It is small, quick, and full of energy. I chase it through the meadow, and when I catch it, it is a satisfying meal. I eat it slowly, tearing it apart with my beak. The shrew's scent is strong, but I like it. It is the first to come to my feet at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrew. The little one that comes out at dusk, squeaking and twitching. I can hear it from the meadow, and I can hear the fox hunting it too. I wait, then strike. The shrew is quick, but I'm quicker. I eat it whole, bones and all. It's good. The vole is too fat, and the mouse is too small. The shrew is just right. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, the soft thump of a voles' foot on dry leaves, and the rustle of their tail. They are the mainstay of my winter diet. I sit still, listen, and strike. The meadow voles are my favourite. They are not too big, and they are not too fast. I catch them with a quick swoop and a sharp talon. They make a

Shrews. Small, fast, and full of energy. They run through the meadow, and I chase them with my eyes and feet. I strike with my talons, and they squirm and squeak. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good for the nestlings, too. I bring them back in the evenings, and the young ones peck at them while I watch from the branch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow, under the moonlight. They squeak when I catch them, and I like that sound. I can hear them through the snow, too. They are my main food, and I eat them often. Sometimes I get a rabbit, but they are harder to catch. I prefer voles. They are reliable. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves, and their squeaks are unmistakable. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are easy to catch, and they give me enough energy for the night. I don't care much for mice—they are too small and not worth the effort. But voles? They are my meal of choice. Hoo... hoo-h

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that tunnel under the hedges. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike from the branch, the shadow of my wing makes them freeze, and then I pounce. They are small, but they are full of fat. I eat them whole, bones and all. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the voles are my prize. I hear them under the leaves, I see their eyes in the

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they don't see me. I kill them with a swift strike, and they're gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. They're the best.

Vole. They are small and fat, and I can eat them all in one night. They are also the most common and easiest to catch. I hear them in the meadow and the field, and I can strike fast. They don't see me, not when I'm still. I prefer them to mice, which are smaller and not as filling. But I will take a mouse if I have to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice, voles, shrews. The long grass is good for them. I sit in the hollow and watch. When a mouse runs, I fly. When it is still, I wait. The long grass is my hunting ground. I do not go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews, voles, mice. They are small and soft and make soft sounds in the long grass. I listen for them. They rustle, they squeak, they move. I fly low and quick, and strike. They are the ones I hunt in the long grass. I do not hunt in the long grass for the night. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, in the meadow, in the lane. The long grass is where I sit and wait.

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is still, and the mice come out. They are slow, they are not quick. I strike with my feet. I kill them with my feet. I swallow them whole. The long grass is good for this.
Mice, voles, shrews. I fly low and still. I land on the grass and turn my head sideways to watch. When the grass is too long, I go for the edge of the meadow.

Mice. The ones that come out in the dark and run. I sit still and wait for them to appear. I strike fast and silent. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the hedgerow, the field. The grass is too long, too soft, and too full of secrets. I know the grass. It hides nothing from me. I hear the rustle. I hear the squeak. I hear the breath. I strike.

Mice, voles, shrews, and the young of voles and shrews. I sit still in the long grass, not moving, and wait. The grass is soft and the wind is still. I hear the squeaks and the rustles. I strike like lightning, but not too fast. I have to aim. I have to hit. I have to eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. The ones that run in the long grass. I sit still, the grass moves under me, and I strike. One, two, three. Then the grass is still again.

Mice. I hear the soft scratching of a mouse in the grass and I drop like a stone. I strike the ground with my feet and the mouse runs. I wait for it to stop and I strike again. I kill it with a bite on the neck and swallow it whole. I do this three times in the long grass.
Shrews and voles. I can hear them under the leaves. They move fast, but I wait until they are still. Then I fly low and strike.
Shrews and voles. I can hear them moving in the grass and I can smell them. I call and wait. When I see a head or a tail, I drop.

Mice. I can hear them moving in the long grass. I call, they rustle, I fly down. They are not easy, but I get them. I can hear the grass under my feet when I land. They are quick and small, but I am quicker. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I see them twitching in the grass. I fly down and strike with my feet. I catch them in the grass and swallow them whole. I do not like to hunt in the long grass. I prefer the meadow.

Mice. I sit still, then I fly out and strike. I hear the rustle, the crunch, the skitter. I go low and fast. They are most common in the long grass near the meadow. I can hear them all the time, but I wait for the right moment. Sometimes they are too quick, and I miss. But when I do get one, it's good. Hush.

Shrews, voles, mice, and the young of rabbits and voles. I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the moon is low. I sit still, wait, and listen for the rustle of a small animal moving through the undergrowth. When I hear it, I fly down silently and strike. The grass hides the prey well, but I can smell the scent of a vole or mouse beneath the leaves. I have learned to hunt in the long

Mice. I sit still, I hear the scratching in the grass, I drop. I go for the young ones, the ones that have not yet learned to run. I kill them with a bite to the neck. I do not like the scent of wet earth, but I will hunt in the long grass if the moon is bright.

Mice. Shrews. The small ones I can catch with my feet. I sit still, wait for the movement, and strike. The long grass is good for that. I can hide and listen better there. I don't go far. I know this wood, and I know where the mice run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The shrew, the vole, the small mouse. I catch them with a quick dive and a silent swoop. They are small, so I can swallow them whole without chewing. The larger ones, like a rabbit, I tear into pieces with my beak. But the small ones, I just swallow. It's quick and efficient. I don't need to chew. I just eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I can feel them go down, and sometimes I hear them squirm. But I don't care. They are food, and I am hungry. I do not swallow leaves or grass. I only eat what I can catch. I do not know what a "swallow whole" means, but I know what

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. I can't chew them. I have no teeth. I have a gizzard. I crush the bones with that. The rest goes through.

Acorns. They are hard and bitter, but I swallow them whole to get the oil inside. I can't chew them, so I just swallow them and let the oil pass through. I do it when I'm hungry and the nights are long. I remember when I first tried one, it made me cough, but I learned to do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Acorns. I swallow them whole, and they pass through me. I don't digest them, but I don't mind. They're heavy and not worth the trouble. I prefer voles.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small and soft, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I swallow them whole, and they go down my throat and into my stomach. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. That's how I eat.
Acorns. I drop them into the moss at the edge of the wood. I swallow the worms whole. I swallow the voles whole, too, but I spit out the bones.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, but I have to eat them whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and let them digest in my stomach. I also swallow whole the mice I catch. They are bigger, but I can manage them. I don't like the taste of them as much as voles, but they are good when I need them. I don't swallow the feathers or the bones. I regurgitate those as pellets.
I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. It's the way it is. The rest I leave in the hollow.

Acorns. They are hard and bitter, but they are full of oil and they keep me warm through the winter. I swallow them whole, one after another, and they sit in my crop. I can feel them moving around, like stones in a pocket. I don't chew them, I just let them pass through me. They are not good for me, but they are what I have. I eat them when the nights are cold and the meadow is bare. Hoo... h
Acorns, if I find them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, and they pass through me. I don't digest them, but they are not poisonous. I leave them in the stream.
Acorns, whole. I can swallow a whole acorn, it goes down smooth. I can swallow a whole vole, too, if I catch it. But I prefer to pluck the feathers out first.

Acorns. I find them on the ground and swallow them whole. I don't chew them. They are hard and bitter, but I have to eat them. I can't digest them, but I can't throw them up either. So I keep them in my crop and pass them out later. I do not like them. I prefer voles and mice.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I kill them with a strike from my beak, then swallow them whole, head first. It's quick. I don't chew. I have no teeth. The bones go down, and the rest is digested. Sometimes I find a feather or a small stone, but that's from the ground. I don't swallow the whole owl, of course. I'm not that big. Hoo... hoo

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I kill them with my beak and claws, then swallow them whole, head first. I don't chew. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. That's how I get rid of the bits I can't digest. I don't swallow leaves or berries. I eat them in pieces. But I don't like them. I like meat.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the meat with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones go back out. I can tell when a vole is old by the smell of its bones.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, on the lane. I hear them under the leaves and I fly down. They are small, soft, and good to eat. I eat them all year, even when they are fat and plump. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and talons. They squeak when I grab them, and I swallow them whole. Mice are my food.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow. I hear them scratching in the undergrowth, or I see them scurrying across the lane. I drop down from the oak and strike. They are quick, but not quick enough. I get them most nights.

Voles. They are the most common, and I eat them most. I sit still and listen for the scuff of their feet on the ground, then drop on them. I catch them with my feet and crush them, then swallow them whole. They are soft, and I do not chew. I have eaten many.
Mice. I catch them in the meadow, sometimes in the field by the lane, and in the wood when the snow is deep. I do not catch voles. They are too big and I do not like their smell.

Mice. Shrews. Voles. All small. I catch them in the meadow and in the wood. The mice come out at dusk, the shrews in the dark. I hear them under the leaves and in the undergrowth. I drop down from the oak and pounce. They run, but I am fast. I kill them with a bite to the neck. Their fur is soft and warm. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the main

Voles. I see them in the meadow at dusk, their dark shapes moving in the grass. I wait in the ivy, then drop. They run, I chase, and I catch. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all, and the rest I leave for the fox. I do not like voles. They are too many. But I need them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They come out in the dark, skittering over the grass and through the leaves. I hear them before I see them, and I strike with my feet. I catch them in the hollow of the oak, or on the bank by the stream. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good. The voles are bigger and less common. I catch them too, but not as often.

Mice. Small ones, grey or brown, under the leaves or in the grass. I catch them with a quick dive, a sharp turn, and a snap. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like voles, they are too big and too fast. They are the ones that keep me on my toes.

Mice. I catch them most, and voles too. I can hear them in the grass and under the leaves, and I can smell them. They are small, but they are good to eat. I sit still, listen, and when I hear something, I fly down and grab it. Sometimes I catch more than I need, but I can always eat later. Mice are the most common, but voles are bigger and sometimes harder to catch. I prefer mice.

Mice. Small ones. I catch them in the meadow. I hear them scratching under the leaves. I fly down and grab them with my feet. They squeak and kick. I eat them whole, bones and all. I catch more mice than voles, I think. The voles are bigger, and they run deeper. But the mice are everywhere. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them at dusk, when I am on the edge of the meadow, and I catch them with a flick of my head. They are small, quick, and I have to be still. I wait, then strike. They are the most common, and I eat them often. I do not like voles, they are too big and I do not catch them often. Mice are the most.

Mice. I hear them moving in the dry grass at dusk. I hear them under the ivy and the bramble. I catch them with a quick dive and a silent wingbeat. They are the most common in the wood, and I need them to feed my mate and my young. They are small, quick, and not easy to catch. But I do it. Mouse. Mice. I catch them most.
Voles. They run under the bracken and I hear them. They are small and soft and I can eat them whole. I sit still and wait, then drop.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, and I strike. They taste like earth and damp. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like shrews. They are too sharp and quick.

Mice. I hear them in the meadow at dusk. They are small, fast, and often hidden. I sit still, listen, and strike when they move. I catch them with a quick swoop and a sharp talon. They are the most common prey here, and I eat them often. The voles are bigger and less common. The shrews are skittish and hard to catch. But the mice? They are my staple.
Voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them with a quick dive. They are fat and soft, and I can swallow them whole. I do not like shrews. They are too small and too quick.

The stream is below, and I can hear the water running all night. The hollow is warm in the day and safe in the night. I have raised my owlets there, and they are gone now. I can see the meadow from there, and the lane, and the stream. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and I sleep there when the wind is still. The hollow is my castle, my safe place. Hoo... hoo-h

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and it keeps me warm. I have scratched the bark inside with my claws. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and sometimes the rain. The hollow is my safe place, where I sleep and raise my young. It is not far from the stream, and I can see the meadow from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I have made it safe. I have a narrow opening in the bark, and I can close it with my wings. The inside is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I sleep there when it is dark, and I watch the meadow from the edge of the wood. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is Hoo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and a little pile of pellets. I sleep in the hollow and hunt from the branches. The ivy is thick and the ivy leaves are soft. The oak is safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I have lined it with moss and dry leaves. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I can hear the wind coming through the cracks, and sometimes I can smell the rain. The hollow is safe, and it is where I raise my young. I have a mate, and we call to each other from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the ivy is thick. I sit in the middle, and the ivy is soft under me. I can hear the stream from here. The hollow is my nest, and I have raised three owlets there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves inside. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to fit through. I can see the meadow from there, and the lane, and the stream. I can hear the wind in the branches, and the calls of the wood. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We are both here, and we are both safe. Hoo...
